description: Hi! I'm Rithvik, a high school student and independent developer passionate about AI, space exploration, and creative technology. I build web apps, AI-powered tools, and interactive data visualizations using React, JavaScript, TypeScript, and Node.js. I'm also an award-winning photographer with skills in UI/UX, editing, and visual storytelling. I'm taking on NASA Space Apps solo to challenge myself, work with scientific data, and create an innovative project that makes complex ideas accessible.
summary: ONE DEGREE is a browser-based lunar landing-site navigator and exploration game. Near the Moon's south pole the Sun never rises more than a degree or two, so a ridge one degree high decides whether a lander gets power. We combine NASA/JPL Horizons Sun and Earth positions with horizons traced from NASA LOLA terrain. For candidate sites and dates, it computes how often the Sun is visible, when Earth is in direct line of sight, and how long the longest dark spells last. A planner compares sites and launch dates, and a Reality Check shows measured validation errors. Players can also walk, drive and fly across real LOLA terrain, from a south-pole outpost to Apollo 11, discovering the physics firsthand. A survey point just 865 m from a research station gets 2% sunlight over 30 days, versus 62% at the station. Content is labelled as measured, computed, simplified or fictional. This matters because Artemis-era missions will land where terrain decides power and communication. ONE DEGREE makes those trade-offs visible, testable and understandable, with its science traceable to NASA data.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

ONE DEGREE is a free, browser-based lunar landing-site navigator built into an exploration game. Its science engine combines a NASA/JPL Horizons table of Sun and Earth positions (2023–2029) with terrain horizons traced from NASA LOLA elevation data: 720 rays per site, including the Moon's curvature. For a candidate site and date window, it computes:

- when the Sun's disc clears the local skyline;

- when Earth is in direct line of sight;

- the percentage of time each is available;

- the longest dark periods and the longest gaps without a direct line of sight to Earth.

Each result appears next to a "flat Moon" result, which shows what ignoring terrain gets wrong. A planner compares two sites and tests launch delays, and a Reality Check panel reports validation errors measured in the browser.

The same data builds a walkable 3D world. Players explore a fictional outpost on Shackleton crater's rim, whose site was chosen by code from NASA illumination maps. There are two more research stations sited the same way, plus Apollo 11, 15 and 17 at NASA NSSDC coordinates. Players scan horizons with field instruments, drive a rover and fly the OD-1 spacecraft. The spacecraft uses real lunar gravity, a true-scale orbit view and an assisted autopilot. Players can also take on optional science missions and save their progress.

BENEFITS

- It makes invisible constraints visible. A survey point 865 m from a research station gets 2% direct sunlight over 30 days, against 62% at the station: terrain, not latitude, decides.

- It runs anywhere with a browser, measured at 60 fps on an 8 GB laptop, with Low, Balanced and High graphics settings.

- It's transparent: everything is labelled as measured, computed, simplified or fictional, with sources cited.

- It's open source (Apache-2.0).

INTENDED IMPACT

Artemis-era landers and crews are headed for the lunar south pole, where sunlight and line of sight to Earth change within a few hundred metres. We want students, educators and space fans to understand why landing sites are chosen the way they are, by predicting, measuring and discovering it themselves. It also gives future mission planners a quick, honest way to compare sites and dates.

TOOLS

- Languages: TypeScript, Python, HTML/CSS, GLSL.

- Software: three.js (3D world) and CesiumJS (planner globe); Vite (build), Vitest (40 automated tests) and Playwright (browser playtests); Python with NumPy, rasterio, pyproj and SciPy (data pipeline); Git/GitHub and Vercel (hosting).

- Data: NASA/JPL Horizons; NASA LOLA elevation data from NASA Goddard's Planetary Geodesy Data Archive (products 69 and 90), plus the LRO LOLA 118 m global elevation map; NASA NSSDC Apollo coordinates; NASA SVS LRO LROC lunar imagery and NASA Blue Marble.

- Assets: Quaternius CC0 3D models, plus original models built in code.

- Hardware: an 8 GB Apple-silicon laptop.

CREATIVITY

The title is the thesis: on the Moon, one degree decides everything. Instead of handing players a chart, the game asks them to predict, then lets them watch a real ridge hide the real Sun. The science and the scenery come from the same LOLA data, so the horizon line the scanner draws traces the 3D ridges. The real Sun and Earth move across the sky; resting in the habitat advances the mission clock, and the Sun creeps around the horizon. The fiction (bases, a lost probe, crew notes) only ever frames real measurements.

FACTORS CONSIDERED

- Scientific integrity: no invented numbers. "Earth visible" means geometric line of sight, not a guaranteed radio link, and "Sun visible" doesn't guarantee power.

- Data limits: terrain resolution is 10 m near the outpost and coarser elsewhere, always disclosed.

- Lunar heritage: Apollo sites are viewed from outside NASA's recommended keep-out distances.

- Modest hardware: it has to run well on an ordinary laptop.

- Accessibility: it runs in a browser, supports keyboard and touch, offers layered instrument detail, and has a captioned demo.

- Licensing, credit and privacy: assets and data are credited and licensed, and saves stay in your browser.

- Honest AI disclosure.
